messages.subject: [R-sig-Geo] [SpatialML] grf.bw tends to select the lower bound of the bandwidth range
messages.subject_clean: [SpatialML] grf.bw tends to select the lower bound of the bandwidth range
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I am using the SpatialML package (geographical random forests) and have a question about bandwidth selection with grf.bw().

When I select the bandwidth that maximises the local R-squared, I almost always end up with the smallest value in the range I test. In my latest run (adaptive kernel, 50 to 400 nearest neighbours), the local R-squared is noisy from one bandwidth to the next, but its overall trend falls steadily as the bandwidth grows: from about 0.25 at 50 neighbours to about 0.20 at 100, and then levelling off around 0.155 between 300 and 400. The maximum therefore lands at or very near the lower bound, and when I lower that bound (e.g. to 10 neighbours), the selected bandwidth moves down with it. By contrast, when I fit other geographically weighted models (e.g. GWR) to the same data, the optimal bandwidths are considerably larger.

In Georganos et al. (2021), "A Forest of Forests: A Spatially Weighted and Computationally Efficient Formulation of Geographical Random Forests", the authors used a range of 20 to 50 nearest neighbours as a proof of concept and noted that smaller bandwidths can give unstable results, because the local sub-models are trained on too few observations. With the 264 NUTS-2 regions in that example, 20-50 neighbours correspond to roughly 7.6-18.9% of the data. My dataset has 1068 observations, and I am concerned that the small bandwidths selected in my case may produce unstable local models.

I would be grateful for any guidance on the following points:

1. Is there a recommended way to set the minimum and maximum of the search range for grf.bw()? For instance, would it be reasonable to define the range as a proportion of the sample size (in my case roughly 81-202 neighbours, mirroring the proportions in the package authors' paper)?

2. How should one interpret the local R-squared favouring the smallest bandwidths? Could this reflect overfitting, with the local forests fitting the few observations in each small neighbourhood too closely, so that the bandwidth should be chosen on other grounds?

Thank you very much for your time. Any suggestions, references, or experiences with similar behaviour would be much appreciated.
